3: Unlike Gas and Coal Plants, which can be located close to a population, wind and solar farms need lots of land. That means they’ll likely be in remote rural locations.
7: New Zealand tells us the future of what will happen when we have 80%+ renewables. That is because New Zealand already faces this “where” problem with renewables, albeit hydro, not solar&wind. In New Zealand,  the largest hydro generation happens [[2|on the South Island]]. But the bulk of the consumption of that electricity happens [[3|on the North Island]].
8: Because of this, it is becoming hard to regulate voltage. It is so hard that the Commerce Commission has just mandated that Transpower, the state-owned company responsible for electricity transmission, must solve this before it becomes an issue. The likely solution is a $100M “STATCOM”. It serves no other useful purpose than to regulate voltage for the 1% of the year when voltage may need regulating, because so much power is moving from one part of the country to another. The other 99% of the time, this widget serves no useful purpose. It doesn’t generate electricity, nor does it help in any way with demand response (see 2. below).
9: So this isn’t the real solution. The real solution is to do a lot of power generation in the middle of the North Island. This location has no large industry, no large population base and no rivers suitable for hydro-power. There is however a lot of land, sun and wind. So the only suitable solution would most likely be solar and wind generation. But this new generation would need a location-agnostic customer. A 50MW solar farm with a data center mining Bitcoin would provide the perfect solution. It would balance voltage, while also generating more power and helping with the “when” problem. In the next section, we’ll look at why having a big battery isn’t enough.
10: The most obvious issue with solar&wind is that solar produces power during the day. But most power is needed for a short morning and evening peak, when the sun is either mostly or completely absent. Wind can produce throughout the day but is very unpredictable.
13: When the battery is full, the battery is full! You can’t continue charging it. Batteries are like a reserve tank on a motorcycle. They can only provide a 2<sup>nd</sup>-tier of support to store excess supply from solar and wind, and their capacity is finite. Batteries therefore cannot stop the wasted-power issue with solar&wind, although they can limit the waste.
14: When a Bitcoin miner stands alongside that battery, however, spare power can be bought by Bitcoin miners. Older “S9” miners are perfect for this. They cost around $200, so they can sit idle most of the day. Then they can be fired up for a few hours in the middle of the day, when demand is low and that power would otherwise have been wasted.
15: These batteries will then need to discharge that power back to the grid as soon as possible, so they can be re-used. But what if wholesale electricity prices have dipped when the battery is full? The cost of absorbing that power could be more than the money the battery makes selling it back to the grid.  Buying power for solar&wind farms and selling it back to the grid is known as “simple arbitrage”. As we can see, it is economically risky.
19: Batteries use not one but several rare metals in their construction (lithium, cobalt, nickel).  Most of these minerals are being mined for EV batteries. So many energy engineers now doubt that enough utility-scale batteries can be built to meet the huge load-balancing and demand-response needs of a solar&wind based grid.
22: 99% of the year, the grid has no issues with meeting demand. But for the remaining 1% of the time, demand spikes and grid operators are left urgently trying to balance supply and demand. In the past, they’ve done this using “peaker plants” – a fossil fuel plant using a gas turbine that comes on when the extra capacity is needed. The problem is that some of this gas-fired backup has to be kept running 24x7 as ‘spinning reserve’ (emitting CO<sub>2</sub> and wasting gas the whole time). It runs just for these rare events, so that it can ramp up energy production quickly.
23: There have been calls from various environmental groups to phase out peaker plants. However, this needs a carefully thought-out strategy, so that users of the grid are not exposed to the blackouts and grid instability that peaker plants help prevent.
24: With batteries, they can dump their power into the grid to lessen the grid’s need for this peaker plant. With Bitcoin miners operating as well, however, the grid gets 2x the benefit: batteries dump power and Bitcoin miners shut off and stop using power at the same time. Bitcoin mining has another advantage. Batteries cannot dispatch all their power to the grid immediately, but Bitcoin miners can be shut off immediately. That gives grid operators more flexibility in dealing with peak demand.
27: In the US, over the decade and more before covid, new gas plants seeking a grid connection were [[6|about twice as likely]] to be completed as solar/wind farms. The reasons were largely the “when/where” issues with solar and wind, which battery storage + Bitcoin mining can largely, if not completely, resolve.
38: Critically, this is not an outcome that battery technology can achieve alone. But it is possible with the twin support of Battery and Bitcoin mining, powering the widespread adoption of solar & wind power.
